questiontext.text:
Match the redox terms in the left column with their electronic definitions in the right column:

TermElectronic Definition
1. OxidationP. Donor of electron(s)
2. ReductionQ. Loss of electron(s) by any species
3. Oxidising agentR. Acceptor of electron(s)
4. Reducing agentS. Gain of electron(s) by any species

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In the electronic concept of redox reactions, oxidation and reduction are defined in terms of the transfer of electrons between interacting species.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Term
1. Oxidation is the loss of electron(s) by any species (matches Q).
2. Reduction is the gain of electron(s) by any species (matches S).
3. An oxidising agent (oxidant) is a species that accepts electron(s) from another species and itself gets reduced (matches R).
4. A reducing agent (reductant) is a species that donates electron(s) to another species and itself gets oxidised (matches P).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Combining these conceptual definitions gives the correct pairing: 1-Q, 2-S, 3-R, 4-P.

questiontext.text:
Match each chemical formula with its correct Stock notation representation:

CompoundStock Notation
1. \(\mathrm{HAuCl_4}\)P. \(\mathrm{Fe_2(III)O_3}\)
2. \(\mathrm{Tl_2O}\)Q. \(\mathrm{HAu(III)Cl_4}\)
3. \(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}\)R. \(\mathrm{Mn(IV)O_2}\)
4. \(\mathrm{MnO_2}\)S. \(\mathrm{Tl_2(I)O}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The four neutral compounds are \(\mathrm{HAuCl_4}\), \(\mathrm{Tl_2O}\), \(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}\), and \(\mathrm{MnO_2}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
In Stock notation, the oxidation number of the metal is written as a Roman numeral in parentheses immediately after the symbol of the metal. Here, \(\mathrm{H} = +1\), \(\mathrm{Cl} = -1\), and \(\mathrm{O} = -2\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The algebraic sum of oxidation numbers of all atoms in a neutral compound is zero.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. In \(\mathrm{HAuCl_4}\): \((+1) + x + 4(-1) = 0 \implies x = +3\), giving \(\mathrm{HAu(III)Cl_4}\) (matches Q).
2. In \(\mathrm{Tl_2O}\): \(2x + (-2) = 0 \implies x = +1\), giving \(\mathrm{Tl_2(I)O}\) (matches S).
3. In \(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}\): \(2x + 3(-2) = 0 \implies x = +3\), giving \(\mathrm{Fe_2(III)O_3}\) (matches P).
4. In \(\mathrm{MnO_2}\): \(x + 2(-2) = 0 \implies x = +4\), giving \(\mathrm{Mn(IV)O_2}\) (matches R).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Each Roman numeral matches the calculated oxidation state of the metal. Thus, the correct pairing is 1-Q, 2-S, 3-P, 4-R.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_REDOXREACTIONS_MATCH_Q03 - Oxidation number of oxygen in compounds

questiontext.text:
Match each compound with the oxidation number of oxygen in it:

CompoundOxidation Number of Oxygen
1. \(\mathrm{H_2O_2}\)P. \(-\frac{1}{2}\)
2. \(\mathrm{KO_2}\)Q. \(+1\)
3. \(\mathrm{OF_2}\)R. \(-1\)
4. \(\mathrm{O_2F_2}\)S. \(+2\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The four compounds are hydrogen peroxide (\(\mathrm{H_2O_2}\)), potassium superoxide (\(\mathrm{KO_2}\)), oxygen difluoride (\(\mathrm{OF_2}\)), and dioxygen difluoride (\(\mathrm{O_2F_2}\)).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Hydrogen has an oxidation number of \(+1\) when bonded to non-metals, potassium (an alkali metal) has \(+1\), and fluorine always has \(-1\) in all its compounds.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The sum of oxidation numbers of all atoms in a neutral molecule equals zero.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. In \(\mathrm{H_2O_2}\) (a peroxide): \(2(+1) + 2x = 0 \implies 2x = -2 \implies x = -1\) (matches R).
2. In \(\mathrm{KO_2}\) (a superoxide): \((+1) + 2x = 0 \implies 2x = -1 \implies x = -\frac{1}{2}\) (matches P).
3. In \(\mathrm{OF_2}\): \(x + 2(-1) = 0 \implies x = +2\) (matches S).
4. In \(\mathrm{O_2F_2}\): \(2x + 2(-1) = 0 \implies 2x = +2 \implies x = +1\) (matches Q).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
All four values represent the standard exceptions to oxygen's usual \(-2\) oxidation state. Thus, the correct pairing is 1-R, 2-P, 3-S, 4-Q.

questiontext.text:
Match each redox reaction with its correct reaction type:

Redox ReactionReaction Type
1. \(\mathrm{N_2(g)} + \mathrm{O_2(g)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NO(g)}\)P. Decomposition reaction
2. \(2\mathrm{Pb(NO_3)_2(s)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{PbO(s)} + 4\mathrm{NO_2(g)} + \mathrm{O_2(g)}\)Q. Disproportionation reaction
3. \(\mathrm{NaH(s)} + \mathrm{H_2O(l)} \rightarrow \mathrm{NaOH(aq)} + \mathrm{H_2(g)}\)R. Displacement reaction
4. \(2\mathrm{NO_2(g)} + 2\mathrm{OH^-(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{NO_2^-(aq)} + \mathrm{NO_3^-(aq)} + \mathrm{H_2O(l)}\)S. Combination reaction

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Redox reactions are classified into four types: combination (elements combine to form a compound), decomposition (a compound breaks down with at least one elemental product), displacement (an atom or ion in a compound is replaced by another), and disproportionation (a single element in an intermediate oxidation state is simultaneously oxidised and reduced).

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Reaction
1. In \(\mathrm{N_2(g)} + \mathrm{O_2(g)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NO(g)}\), elemental nitrogen and oxygen combine to form nitric oxide, making it a combination reaction (matches S).
2. In \(2\mathrm{Pb(NO_3)_2(s)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{PbO(s)} + 4\mathrm{NO_2(g)} + \mathrm{O_2(g)}\), lead nitrate breaks down into three products including elemental \(\mathrm{O_2}\), making it a decomposition reaction (matches P).
3. In \(\mathrm{NaH(s)} + \mathrm{H_2O(l)} \rightarrow \mathrm{NaOH(aq)} + \mathrm{H_2(g)}\), hydrogen of water is displaced by hydride ion to form dihydrogen gas, making it a displacement reaction (matches R).
4. In \(2\mathrm{NO_2(g)} + 2\mathrm{OH^-(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{NO_2^-(aq)} + \mathrm{NO_3^-(aq)} + \mathrm{H_2O(l)}\), nitrogen in \(\mathrm{NO_2}\) (\(+4\)) is simultaneously reduced to \(\mathrm{NO_2^-}\) (\(+3\)) and oxidised to \(\mathrm{NO_3^-}\) (\(+5\)), making it a disproportionation reaction (matches Q).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the correct matching is 1-S, 2-P, 3-R, 4-Q.

questiontext.text:
Match each species with the oxidation number of the specified element in it:

Species and ElementOxidation Number
1. Phosphorus in \(\mathrm{NaH_2PO_4}\)P. \(+3\)
2. Manganese in \(\mathrm{K_2MnO_4}\)Q. \(+5\)
3. Boron in \(\mathrm{NaBH_4}\)R. \(+7\)
4. Manganese in \(\mathrm{MnO_4^-}\)S. \(+6\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
We need to determine the oxidation numbers of \(\mathrm{P}\) in \(\mathrm{NaH_2PO_4}\), \(\mathrm{Mn}\) in \(\mathrm{K_2MnO_4}\), \(\mathrm{B}\) in \(\mathrm{NaBH_4}\), and \(\mathrm{Mn}\) in \(\mathrm{MnO_4^-}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Alkali metals (\(\mathrm{Na, K}\)) have oxidation number \(+1\), oxygen has \(-2\), hydrogen has \(+1\) with non-metals and \(-1\) in binary/complex metal hydrides (\(\mathrm{BH_4^-}\)).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The algebraic sum of oxidation numbers equals \(0\) for neutral compounds and equals the ionic charge for polyatomic ions.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. In \(\mathrm{NaH_2PO_4}\): \((+1) + 2(+1) + x + 4(-2) = 0 \implies 3 + x - 8 = 0 \implies x = +5\) (matches Q).
2. In \(\mathrm{K_2MnO_4}\): \(2(+1) + x + 4(-2) = 0 \implies 2 + x - 8 = 0 \implies x = +6\) (matches S).
3. In \(\mathrm{NaBH_4}\): \((+1) + x + 4(-1) = 0 \implies 1 + x - 4 = 0 \implies x = +3\) (matches P).
4. In \(\mathrm{MnO_4^-}\): \(x + 4(-2) = -1 \implies x - 8 = -1 \implies x = +7\) (matches R).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
All four calculations are consistent with standard oxidation number rules. Thus, the correct pairing is 1-Q, 2-S, 3-P, 4-R.

questiontext.text:
Match each species with the average oxidation number of the specified element:

Species and ElementAverage Oxidation Number
1. Iodine in \(\mathrm{KI_3}\)P. \(+2.5\)
2. Sulphur in \(\mathrm{H_2S_4O_6}\)Q. \(+\frac{4}{3}\)
3. Iron in \(\mathrm{Fe_3O_4}\)R. \(-\frac{1}{3}\)
4. Carbon in \(\mathrm{C_3O_2}\)S. \(+\frac{8}{3}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
We need the average oxidation number of \(\mathrm{I}\) in \(\mathrm{KI_3}\), \(\mathrm{S}\) in \(\mathrm{H_2S_4O_6}\), \(\mathrm{Fe}\) in \(\mathrm{Fe_3O_4}\), and \(\mathrm{C}\) in \(\mathrm{C_3O_2}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Using standard rules, \(\mathrm{K} = +1\), \(\mathrm{H} = +1\), and \(\mathrm{O} = -2\). When a compound contains multiple atoms of an element in different oxidation states, the algebraic formula gives the average oxidation number.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
For any neutral compound, \(\sum (\text{oxidation number}) = 0\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. In \(\mathrm{KI_3}\): \((+1) + 3x = 0 \implies x = -\frac{1}{3}\) (matches R).
2. In \(\mathrm{H_2S_4O_6}\): \(2(+1) + 4x + 6(-2) = 0 \implies 4x - 10 = 0 \implies x = +\frac{10}{4} = +2.5\) (matches P).
3. In \(\mathrm{Fe_3O_4}\): \(3x + 4(-2) = 0 \implies 3x = +8 \implies x = +\frac{8}{3}\) (matches S).
4. In \(\mathrm{C_3O_2}\): \(3x + 2(-2) = 0 \implies 3x = +4 \implies x = +\frac{4}{3}\) (matches Q).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Each fractional value represents the average oxidation state across all atoms of that element in the species. Thus, the correct pairing is 1-R, 2-P, 3-S, 4-Q.

questiontext.text:
Match each Period 3 group and representative compound with the highest oxidation number state exhibited by the group element:

Group and CompoundHighest Oxidation Number
1. Group 13 (\(\mathrm{AlF_3}\))P. \(+6\)
2. Group 15 (\(\mathrm{P_4O_{10}}\))Q. \(+5\)
3. Group 16 (\(\mathrm{SF_6}\))R. \(+7\)
4. Group 17 (\(\mathrm{HClO_4}\))S. \(+3\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
We are given four Period 3 elements in their highest oxidation state compounds: \(\mathrm{AlF_3}\) (Group 13), \(\mathrm{P_4O_{10}}\) (Group 15), \(\mathrm{SF_6}\) (Group 16), and \(\mathrm{HClO_4}\) (Group 17).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The highest oxidation number of a representative element in Groups 13 to 17 is equal to \((\text{group number} - 10)\). Also, \(\mathrm{F} = -1\), \(\mathrm{O} = -2\), and \(\mathrm{H} = +1\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Sum of oxidation numbers in a neutral molecule \(= 0\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. Group 13 (\(\mathrm{Al}\) in \(\mathrm{AlF_3}\)): \(13 - 10 = +3\), and \(x + 3(-1) = 0 \implies x = +3\) (matches S).
2. Group 15 (\(\mathrm{P}\) in \(\mathrm{P_4O_{10}}\)): \(15 - 10 = +5\), and \(4x + 10(-2) = 0 \implies x = +5\) (matches Q).
3. Group 16 (\(\mathrm{S}\) in \(\mathrm{SF_6}\)): \(16 - 10 = +6\), and \(x + 6(-1) = 0 \implies x = +6\) (matches P).
4. Group 17 (\(\mathrm{Cl}\) in \(\mathrm{HClO_4}\)): \(17 - 10 = +7\), and \((+1) + x + 4(-2) = 0 \implies x = +7\) (matches R).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Both the periodic group rule and direct formula calculation yield identical results. Thus, the correct pairing is 1-S, 2-Q, 3-P, 4-R.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_REDOXREACTIONS_MATCH_Q08 - Oxidation state behaviour of Cs, Ne, I, and F

questiontext.text:
Match each element with its characteristic oxidation state behaviour in compounds:

ElementOxidation State Behaviour
1. Fluorine (\(\mathrm{F}\))P. Exhibits both positive and negative oxidation states
2. Caesium (\(\mathrm{Cs}\))Q. Exhibits only negative oxidation state
3. Iodine (\(\mathrm{I}\))R. Exhibits neither positive nor negative oxidation state
4. Neon (\(\mathrm{Ne}\))S. Exhibits only positive oxidation state

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The oxidation states an element can exhibit depend on its electronegativity, metallic/non-metallic character, and electronic configuration.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Element
1. Fluorine (\(\mathrm{F}\)) is the most electronegative element in the periodic table, so in all its compounds it exhibits only a negative oxidation state of \(-1\) (matches Q).
2. Caesium (\(\mathrm{Cs}\)) is a highly electropositive alkali metal, so in all its compounds it exhibits only a positive oxidation state of \(+1\) (matches S).
3. Iodine (\(\mathrm{I}\)) is a halogen that forms iodides (\(-1\)) as well as oxoacids and oxoanions (\(+1, +5, +7\)), so it exhibits both positive and negative oxidation states (matches P).
4. Neon (\(\mathrm{Ne}\)) is an inert noble gas with a completely filled valence shell that does not form compounds, so it exhibits neither positive nor negative oxidation states (matches R).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the correct matching is 1-Q, 2-S, 3-P, 4-R.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_REDOXREACTIONS_MATCH_Q09 - Indicators and detection in redox titrations

questiontext.text:
Match each redox titration or qualitative test with its end-point detection method:

Redox SystemDetection / Indicator
1. \(\mathrm{MnO_4^-}\) titration against \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\)P. Diphenylamine (intense blue colour)
2. \(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}\) titrationQ. Layer test (colour of halogen in \(\mathrm{CCl_4}\))
3. \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) / \(\mathrm{I^-}\) titration with \(\mathrm{S_2O_3^{2-}}\)R. Self-indicator (lasting pink tinge at \(10^{-6}\text{ mol dm}^{-3}\))
4. \(\mathrm{Br^-}\) / \(\mathrm{I^-}\) displacement by \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\)S. Starch (blue colour disappears at end point)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Redox titrations and halogen displacement tests use either self-indicators, external redox-sensitive indicators, starch-iodine complexation, or organic solvent extraction to detect reaction completion.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each System
1. Permanganate ion (\(\mathrm{MnO_4^-}\)) is intensely coloured and acts as a self-indicator, producing a lasting pink tinge at concentrations as low as \(10^{-6}\text{ mol dm}^{-3}\) just after the equivalence point (matches R).
2. Dichromate ion (\(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}\)) lacks a sharp auto-colour change, so it oxidises diphenylamine just after the equivalence point to produce an intense blue colour (matches P).
3. In iodometric estimation of \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\), liberated \(\mathrm{I_2}\) forms an intense blue colour with starch, which disappears once \(\mathrm{I_2}\) is completely consumed by \(\mathrm{S_2O_3^{2-}}\) (matches S).
4. When \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) displaces \(\mathrm{Br_2}\) or \(\mathrm{I_2}\) from \(\mathrm{Br^-}\) or \(\mathrm{I^-}\), the liberated halogens dissolve in \(\mathrm{CCl_4}\) to give characteristic colours in the Layer Test (matches Q).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the correct matching is 1-R, 2-P, 3-S, 4-Q.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_REDOXREACTIONS_MATCH_Q10 - Non-metal displacement of hydrogen by metals

questiontext.text:
Match each metal with its characteristic reactivity towards water, steam, and hydrochloric acid:

MetalReactivity Behaviour
1. Sodium (\(\mathrm{Na}\))P. Does not react with steam, but displaces \(\mathrm{H_2}\) from acids
2. Iron (\(\mathrm{Fe}\))Q. Displaces \(\mathrm{H_2}\) from cold water
3. Cadmium (\(\mathrm{Cd}\))R. Does not react even with hydrochloric acid
4. Gold (\(\mathrm{Au}\))S. Reacts with steam to produce \(\mathrm{H_2}\) gas

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The ability of a metal to displace dihydrogen (\(\mathrm{H_2}\)) from water, steam, or acids reflects its reducing strength in the metal activity series.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Metal
1. Alkali metals like sodium (\(\mathrm{Na}\)) are very strong reductants and displace \(\mathrm{H_2}\) from cold water: \(2\mathrm{Na(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O(l)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NaOH(aq)} + \mathrm{H_2(g)}\) (matches Q).
2. Less active metals such as iron (\(\mathrm{Fe}\)) do not react with cold water but react with steam to produce \(\mathrm{H_2}\) gas: \(2\mathrm{Fe(s)} + 3\mathrm{H_2O(l)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{Fe_2O_3(s)} + 3\mathrm{H_2(g)}\) (matches S).
3. Cadmium (\(\mathrm{Cd}\)) and tin do not react with steam, yet they are capable of displacing \(\mathrm{H_2}\) from acids (matches P).
4. Very less active native metals such as gold (\(\mathrm{Au}\)) and silver (\(\mathrm{Ag}\)) do not react even with hydrochloric acid (matches R).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the correct matching is 1-Q, 2-S, 3-P, 4-R.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_REDOXREACTIONS_MATCH_Q11 - Identifying reducing agents in redox equations

questiontext.text:
Match each redox reaction with the species acting as the reducing agent (reductant):

Redox ReactionReducing Agent
1. \(\mathrm{HCHO(l)} + 2\mathrm{[Ag(NH_3)_2]^+(aq)} + 3\mathrm{OH^-(aq)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Ag(s)} + \mathrm{HCOO^-(aq)} + 4\mathrm{NH_3(aq)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O(l)}\)P. \(\mathrm{N_2H_4}\)
2. \(\mathrm{N_2H_4(l)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O_2(l)} \rightarrow \mathrm{N_2(g)} + 4\mathrm{H_2O(l)}\)Q. \(\mathrm{Pb(s)}\)
3. \(2\mathrm{Cu_2O(s)} + \mathrm{Cu_2S(s)} \rightarrow 6\mathrm{Cu(s)} + \mathrm{SO_2(g)}\)R. \(\mathrm{HCHO}\)
4. \(\mathrm{Pb(s)} + \mathrm{PbO_2(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_2SO_4(aq)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{PbSO_4(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O(l)}\)S. \(\mathrm{Cu_2S}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A reducing agent (reductant) is the species that undergoes oxidation (an increase in oxidation number of one of its elements) while reducing another species.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Reaction
1. In \(\mathrm{HCHO} \rightarrow \mathrm{HCOO^-}\), carbon's oxidation number increases from \(0\) to \(+2\) while \(\mathrm{Ag^+}\) is reduced to \(\mathrm{Ag(s)}\); thus, \(\mathrm{HCHO}\) is the reducing agent (matches R).
2. In \(\mathrm{N_2H_4} \rightarrow \mathrm{N_2}\), nitrogen's oxidation number increases from \(-2\) to \(0\) while oxygen in \(\mathrm{H_2O_2}\) is reduced from \(-1\) to \(-2\); thus, \(\mathrm{N_2H_4}\) is the reducing agent (matches P).
3. In \(2\mathrm{Cu_2O} + \mathrm{Cu_2S} \rightarrow 6\mathrm{Cu} + \mathrm{SO_2}\), sulphur in \(\mathrm{Cu_2S}\) is oxidised from \(-2\) to \(+4\) while \(\mathrm{Cu(I)}\) is reduced to \(0\); thus, \(\mathrm{Cu_2S}\) acts as the reducing agent (matches S).
4. In \(\mathrm{Pb(s)} + \mathrm{PbO_2(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_2SO_4(aq)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{PbSO_4(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O(l)}\), \(\mathrm{Pb(s)}\) is oxidised from \(0\) to \(+2\) in \(\mathrm{PbSO_4}\) while \(\mathrm{PbO_2}\) (\(+4\)) is reduced to \(+2\); thus, \(\mathrm{Pb(s)}\) is the reducing agent (matches Q).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the correct matching is 1-R, 2-P, 3-S, 4-Q.

questiontext.text:
Match each disproportionation reaction with the oxidation state change of the element undergoing disproportionation:

Disproportionation ReactionOxidation State Change
1. \(\mathrm{P_4(s)} + 3\mathrm{OH^-(aq)} + 3\mathrm{H_2O(l)} \rightarrow \mathrm{PH_3(g)} + 3\mathrm{H_2PO_2^-(aq)}\)P. \(0 \rightarrow -2\text{ and }+2\)
2. \(\mathrm{S_8(s)} + 12\mathrm{OH^-(aq)} \rightarrow 4\mathrm{S^{2-}(aq)} + 2\mathrm{S_2O_3^{2-}(aq)} + 6\mathrm{H_2O(l)}\)Q. \(+4 \rightarrow +3\text{ and }+5\)
3. \(6\mathrm{ClO_2^-(aq)} \xrightarrow{h\nu} 4\mathrm{ClO_3^-(aq)} + 2\mathrm{Cl^-(aq)}\)R. \(0 \rightarrow -3\text{ and }+1\)
4. \(2\mathrm{NO_2(g)} + 2\mathrm{OH^-(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{NO_2^-(aq)} + \mathrm{NO_3^-(aq)} + \mathrm{H_2O(l)}\)S. \(+3 \rightarrow +5\text{ and }-1\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
We are given four disproportionation reactions involving \(\mathrm{P_4}\), \(\mathrm{S_8}\), \(\mathrm{ClO_2^-}\), and \(\mathrm{NO_2}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Standard oxidation numbers are \(\mathrm{H} = +1\) (with non-metals) and \(\mathrm{O} = -2\); uncombined elements have oxidation number \(0\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The algebraic sum of oxidation numbers equals \(0\) for molecules and equals the net charge for ions.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. For \(\mathrm{P_4}\) reaction: \(\mathrm{P}\) in \(\mathrm{P_4}\) is \(0\). In \(\mathrm{PH_3}\): \(x + 3(+1) = 0 \implies x = -3\). In \(\mathrm{H_2PO_2^-}\): \(2(+1) + x + 2(-2) = -1 \implies x = +1\). Change: \(0 \rightarrow -3\text{ and }+1\) (matches R).
2. For \(\mathrm{S_8}\) reaction: \(\mathrm{S}\) in \(\mathrm{S_8}\) is \(0\). In \(\mathrm{S^{2-}}\), it is \(-2\). In \(\mathrm{S_2O_3^{2-}}\): \(2x + 3(-2) = -2 \implies x = +2\). Change: \(0 \rightarrow -2\text{ and }+2\) (matches P).
3. For \(\mathrm{ClO_2^-}\) reaction: \(\mathrm{Cl}\) in \(\mathrm{ClO_2^-}\) is \(x + 2(-2) = -1 \implies x = +3\). In \(\mathrm{ClO_3^-}\): \(x + 3(-2) = -1 \implies x = +5\). In \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\), it is \(-1\). Change: \(+3 \rightarrow +5\text{ and }-1\) (matches S).
4. For \(\mathrm{NO_2}\) reaction: \(\mathrm{N}\) in \(\mathrm{NO_2}\) is \(+4\). In \(\mathrm{NO_2^-}\): \(x + 2(-2) = -1 \implies x = +3\). In \(\mathrm{NO_3^-}\): \(x + 3(-2) = -1 \implies x = +5\). Change: \(+4 \rightarrow +3\text{ and }+5\) (matches Q).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Each reaction shows simultaneous increase and decrease in oxidation state. Thus, the correct pairing is 1-R, 2-P, 3-S, 4-Q.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_REDOXREACTIONS_MATCH_Q13 - Stoichiometric ratios in balanced redox equations

questiontext.text:
Match each skeletal redox reaction with the stoichiometric mole ratio of oxidant to reductant in its balanced ionic equation:

Skeletal Redox ReactionOxidant : Reductant Ratio
1. \(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}(aq)} + \mathrm{SO_3^{2-}(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cr^{3+}(aq)} + \mathrm{SO_4^{2-}(aq)}\) (acidic)P. \(1 : 6\)
2. \(\mathrm{MnO_4^-(aq)} + \mathrm{Br^-(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{MnO_2(s)} + \mathrm{BrO_3^-(aq)}\) (basic)Q. \(1 : 3\)
3. \(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}(aq)} + \mathrm{Fe^{2+}(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cr^{3+}(aq)} + \mathrm{Fe^{3+}(aq)}\) (acidic)R. \(2 : 5\)
4. \(\mathrm{MnO_4^-(aq)} + \mathrm{SO_2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Mn^{2+}(aq)} + \mathrm{HSO_4^-(aq)}\) (acidic)S. \(2 : 1\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
We are given four unbalanced redox reactions in acidic or basic medium and need the stoichiometric ratio of oxidant to reductant.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
In a balanced redox equation, the total decrease in oxidation number of the oxidant must equal the total increase in oxidation number of the reductant.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\(n_{\text{oxidant}} \times (\Delta\text{O.N. per formula unit of oxidant}) = n_{\text{reductant}} \times (\Delta\text{O.N. per formula unit of reductant})\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. \(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}} + \mathrm{SO_3^{2-}}\): Each \(\mathrm{Cr}\) decreases by \(3\) (\(+6 \rightarrow +3\)), so \(1\text{ }\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}\) decreases by \(2 \times 3 = 6\). \(\mathrm{S}\) increases by \(2\) (\(+4 \rightarrow +6\)). Balancing gives \(1\text{ }\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}} : 3\text{ }\mathrm{SO_3^{2-}}\), ratio \(1:3\) (matches Q).
2. \(\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + \mathrm{Br^-}\): \(\mathrm{Mn}\) decreases by \(3\) (\(+7 \rightarrow +4\)). \(\mathrm{Br}\) increases by \(6\) (\(-1 \rightarrow +5\)). Balancing gives \(2\text{ }\mathrm{MnO_4^-} : 1\text{ }\mathrm{Br^-}\), ratio \(2:1\) (matches S).
3. \(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}} + \mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\): \(1\text{ }\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}\) decreases by \(6\), while \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) increases by \(1\) (\(+2 \rightarrow +3\)). Balancing gives \(1\text{ }\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}} : 6\text{ }\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\), ratio \(1:6\) (matches P).
4. \(\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + \mathrm{SO_2}\): \(\mathrm{Mn}\) decreases by \(5\) (\(+7 \rightarrow +2\)), while \(\mathrm{S}\) increases by \(2\) (\(+4 \rightarrow +6\)). Balancing gives \(2\text{ }\mathrm{MnO_4^-} : 5\text{ }\mathrm{SO_2}\), ratio \(2:5\) (matches R).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Total oxidation number changes balance in all four cases. Thus, the correct pairing is 1-Q, 2-S, 3-P, 4-R.

questiontext.text:
Match each reduction half-reaction with its standard electrode potential (\(E^\circ\)) at \(298\text{ K}\):

Reduction Half-Reaction\(E^\circ / \text{V}\)
1. \(\mathrm{F_2(g)} + 2\mathrm{e^-} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{F^-}\)P. \(+1.51\)
2. \(\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + 8\mathrm{H^+} + 5\mathrm{e^-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Mn^{2+}} + 4\mathrm{H_2O}\)Q. \(-3.05\)
3. \(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}} + 14\mathrm{H^+} + 6\mathrm{e^-} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Cr^{3+}} + 7\mathrm{H_2O}\)R. \(+2.87\)
4. \(\mathrm{Li^+} + \mathrm{e^-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Li(s)}\)S. \(+1.33\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Standard electrode potentials (\(E^\circ\)) at \(298\text{ K}\) quantify the relative tendency of oxidised species to accept electrons. Strongest oxidising agents have the highest positive \(E^\circ\) values, while strongest reducing agents have the most negative \(E^\circ\) values.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Half-Reaction
1. \(\mathrm{F_2(g)}\) is the strongest oxidising agent in the electrochemical series, with \(E^\circ(\mathrm{F_2/F^-}) = +2.87\text{ V}\) (matches R).
2. Permanganate ion in acidic medium (\(\mathrm{MnO_4^-/Mn^{2+}}\)) is a strong oxidant with \(E^\circ = +1.51\text{ V}\) (matches P).
3. Dichromate ion in acidic medium (\(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}/Cr^{3+}}\)) has \(E^\circ = +1.33\text{ V}\) (matches S).
4. Lithium (\(\mathrm{Li^+/Li}\)) is the strongest reducing agent among the listed couples, having the most negative \(E^\circ = -3.05\text{ V}\) (matches Q).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the correct matching is 1-R, 2-P, 3-S, 4-Q.

questiontext.text:
Match each aqueous electrolysis setup with the products formed at the cathode and anode, respectively:

Electrolysis SetupProducts (Cathode ; Anode)
1. Aqueous \(\mathrm{AgNO_3}\) with silver electrodesP. \(\mathrm{H_2(g)}\) ; \(\mathrm{O_2(g)}\)
2. Aqueous \(\mathrm{AgNO_3}\) with platinum electrodesQ. \(\mathrm{Ag(s)}\) ; \(\mathrm{O_2(g)}\)
3. Dilute \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) with platinum electrodesR. \(\mathrm{Cu(s)}\) ; \(\mathrm{Cl_2(g)}\)
4. Aqueous \(\mathrm{CuCl_2}\) with platinum electrodesS. \(\mathrm{Ag(s)}\) ; \(\mathrm{Ag^+(aq)}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
During electrolysis, reduction occurs at the cathode and oxidation occurs at the anode. The species discharged depends on standard electrode potentials and whether the electrodes are active or inert.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Setup
1. Aqueous \(\mathrm{AgNO_3}\) with silver electrodes: \(\mathrm{Ag^+}\) is reduced to \(\mathrm{Ag(s)}\) at the cathode, while the active silver anode itself oxidises to \(\mathrm{Ag^+(aq)}\) (matches S).
2. Aqueous \(\mathrm{AgNO_3}\) with inert platinum electrodes: \(\mathrm{Ag^+}\) is reduced to \(\mathrm{Ag(s)}\) at the cathode, while water is oxidised to \(\mathrm{O_2(g)}\) at the anode (matches Q).
3. Dilute \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) with platinum electrodes: \(\mathrm{H^+}\) is reduced to \(\mathrm{H_2(g)}\) at the cathode, while water is oxidised to \(\mathrm{O_2(g)}\) at the anode (matches P).
4. Aqueous \(\mathrm{CuCl_2}\) with platinum electrodes: \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) is reduced to \(\mathrm{Cu(s)}\) at the cathode, while \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\) is oxidised to \(\mathrm{Cl_2(g)}\) at the anode (matches R).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the correct matching is 1-S, 2-Q, 3-P, 4-R.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_REDOXREACTIONS_MATCH_Q16 - Feasibility and standard cell potentials of redox pairs

questiontext.text:
Using the standard reduction potentials at \(298\text{ K}\) [\(E^\circ(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}}) = +0.77\text{ V}\), \(E^\circ(\mathrm{I_2/I^-}) = +0.54\text{ V}\), \(E^\circ(\mathrm{Ag^+/Ag}) = +0.80\text{ V}\), \(E^\circ(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}/Cu}) = +0.34\text{ V}\), \(E^\circ(\mathrm{Br_2/Br^-}) = +1.09\text{ V}\)], match each reactant pair with its feasibility and \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}}\):

Reactant PairFeasibility and \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}}\)
1. \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}(aq)} + \mathrm{I^-(aq)}\)P. Feasible; \(+0.46\text{ V}\)
2. \(\mathrm{Ag^+(aq)} + \mathrm{Cu(s)}\)Q. Feasible; \(+0.32\text{ V}\)
3. \(\mathrm{Ag(s)} + \mathrm{Fe^{3+}(aq)}\)R. Feasible; \(+0.23\text{ V}\)
4. \(\mathrm{Br_2(aq)} + \mathrm{Fe^{2+}(aq)}\)S. Not feasible; \(-0.03\text{ V}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
At \(298\text{ K}\): \(E^\circ(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}}) = +0.77\text{ V}\), \(E^\circ(\mathrm{I_2/I^-}) = +0.54\text{ V}\), \(E^\circ(\mathrm{Ag^+/Ag}) = +0.80\text{ V}\), \(E^\circ(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}/Cu}) = +0.34\text{ V}\), and \(E^\circ(\mathrm{Br_2/Br^-}) = +1.09\text{ V}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
A redox reaction is feasible if \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}} > 0\) and not feasible if \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}} < 0\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{reduction (cathode)}} - E^\circ_{\text{oxidation (anode)}}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}(aq)} + \mathrm{I^-(aq)}\): \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\) is reduced and \(\mathrm{I^-}\) is oxidised, so \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 0.77 - 0.54 = +0.23\text{ V}\) (Feasible; matches R).
2. \(\mathrm{Ag^+(aq)} + \mathrm{Cu(s)}\): \(\mathrm{Ag^+}\) is reduced and \(\mathrm{Cu}\) is oxidised, so \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 0.80 - 0.34 = +0.46\text{ V}\) (Feasible; matches P).
3. \(\mathrm{Ag(s)} + \mathrm{Fe^{3+}(aq)}\): \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\) is reduced and \(\mathrm{Ag}\) is oxidised, so \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 0.77 - 0.80 = -0.03\text{ V}\) (Not feasible; matches S).
4. \(\mathrm{Br_2(aq)} + \mathrm{Fe^{2+}(aq)}\): \(\mathrm{Br_2}\) is reduced and \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) is oxidised, so \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 1.09 - 0.77 = +0.32\text{ V}\) (Feasible; matches Q).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
All four \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}}\) calculations match the feasibility outcomes. Thus, the correct pairing is 1-R, 2-P, 3-S, 4-Q.
